references.text: The institution of the Passover feast in Egypt. John identifies the festival as "the Jews' Passover" (τὸ πάσχα τῶν Ἰουδαίων), which goes back to Exod 12:1-14 where God commands Israel to celebrate Passover as a permanent ordinance.

The command to celebrate Passover and go up to the place the Lord will choose. Deut 16:1-6 requires Israel to keep Passover and sacrifice the Passover lamb at the place the Lord chooses – understood to be Jerusalem, where Jesus now goes up.

The command to appear before the Lord three times a year, including at the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Passover). Deut 16:16 shows the Old Testament background for the pilgrimage journey up to Jerusalem.
The three major pilgrimage festivals, including the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Passover), are established in Exod 23:14-17. Jesus follows this command by going up to Jerusalem.
Another Passover festival is mentioned in John 6:4: "It was near the Passover, the Jews' feast." John structures his gospel around several Passovers; this is the second of three.
The third and final Passover in the Gospel of John is mentioned in John 11:55, where Jesus again goes up to Jerusalem – this time to the Passover at which he himself will be sacrificed as God's lamb.
Luke tells us that Jesus' parents went to Jerusalem every year to celebrate Passover (Luke 2:41-42). Jesus grew up with this tradition of pilgrimage to the temple during the Passover festival.

John the Baptist's testimony about Jesus as "the Lamb of God" in John 1:29 provides a theological framework for Jesus' relationship to Passover. He who is God's Passover lamb now goes up to the temple at the Passover feast.
